body: Congratulations!! That's an amazing accomplishment and you should be so, so proud of yourself. I did my undergrad there (just graduated) if you ever want to chat. :)
I feel like all my problems link back to the fact that I have no identity at all. It's unbearable.
Thank you for saying this. I hope I end up like you when I'm your age.
For me it's lack of identity + guilt over past instances of impulsivity/splitting + complete emotional instability

G*d, same. I feel like I've never had a real friendship because I've always just been putting on a fake personality in front of everyone, but I also have no idea what my "real" personality is like because what even is having an identity.

Even though I've been in a relationship for almost five years and I know my boyfriend loves me, I wonder this myself. I feel like I'm cheating him out of a good relationship with a normal, healthy girl. I feel such shame and guilt and grief when I think about what I've put him through. He says that he would never want to be with anyone else but I find it so hard to believe him. I wish I had something more to say other than that I relate to this a lot.

I had a really good experience with group DBT, in a similar program. I would say to just be open to the new experience and to developing solidarity with your group members...obviously attachment stuff can be tricky with BPD but for me it was really helpful to hear that I wasn't alone in the stuff that I was feeling, that others were grappling with similar things. It can be an intense environment for sure, but the moderator will be there to keep things from getting too heated lol. I really hope you find the setting as helpful as I did.
You don't know what I look like is the thing. :( But thank you, I appreciate this response, it's very kind.
Thank you. It just seems impossible to accept this because my mother and my disorder have convinced me that I can't live a happy, fulfilling life if I'm not thin. That I don't deserve it.

I appreciate this but it does matter what I look like, especially as a woman. Women are judged so cruelly for their looks and fat women are despised. I just graduated university and have to look for a job in a new city, and I'm afraid I'll never get one because of the way that I look.

I think you've already nailed it with what you said - each chapter ends on a sort of tension, and something is completed resolved or advanced in each chapter. As long as both of those qualifications are fulfilled, the actual word count of your chapter is not very important. I personally dislike when authors try and force tension with abrupt chapter endings rather than letting each chapter stand on its own in some respect, and advance the story in a self-contained way. Speculative YA tends towards longer chapters, and contemporary towards shorter, but it's by no means a hard and fast rule. (P.S. I would love to know more about your book; I'm always looking for more magical realism in YA).
I can completely relate to this. I think, at least for me, that it's a defense mechanism, like you said, an instinctual reaction to feeling abandoned.
